title: Unauthenticated request bodies are fully read, JSON-decoded and multipart-spooled before the principal dependency rejects the request
description: agentbox's body routes declare a request-body model - or a File(...) list - together with Depends(principal) / human_only / screen_human (agentbox/api.py:175, 206, 216, 251, 277). In FastAPI's request handler the body is read and JSON-decoded - and on the upload route streamed through request.form() and spooled - before solve_dependencies resolves any of those dependencies, so an unauthenticated client decides how many bytes the control plane buffers, decodes and writes to TMPDIR before it is told 401. Nothing in the tree bounds that work: the only middleware is _NoFraming (api.py:63-80, registered at 113), the serve entry point passes no request-size or concurrency limit to uvicorn (agentbox/cli.py:127), and the shipped Caddy front end has no request_body directive (deploy/Caddyfile:5). The caps that do exist - max_upload_bytes per file (config.py:57, enforced inside the endpoint at api.py:278-283) and LOGGED_ARGS_MAX (service.py:37-38) - run only after a principal exists. Starlette's multipart parser bounds part cardinality (1000 files/fields) and 1 MiB for non-file fields, but not file-part bytes.
root_cause: Authentication dependencies run after FastAPI's body-parsing stage, and nothing in front of the app - ASGI middleware, uvicorn options, or the bundled Caddy reverse proxy - enforces a maximum request-body size, so unauthenticated work scales with the attacker's body size instead of with the negligible work needed to reject an unauthenticated request.
intended_behavior: Requests that cannot yet be authenticated should be rejected before their body is buffered, decoded or written to disk, and bodies above a documented cap should be refused with 413 regardless of credential state.

trace.scope: POST /sandboxes, and every sibling body route: /sandboxes/{sid}/restore (205-206), /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/{tool} (215-216), /approvals/{aid} (250-251), /sandboxes/{sid}/files (276-277)
trace.description: A lower-trust network client with no token reaches a route that declares both a body (CreateSandbox) and Depends(human_only). Declaring the body is what makes FastAPI's handler stage read and JSON-decode the whole request body before any dependency is solved (verified in the installed fastapi 0.161.1 get_request_handler source: body read/decode block precedes the solve_dependencies call).

trace.scope: principal() - first credential check for the JSON API; human_only and screen_human build on it
trace.description: principal() compare_digest's the bearer token (119), looks up an agent token (121) and raises 401 at 117/124. It runs only after the body stage, so no principal exists while the body is buffered and decoded.

files: list[UploadFile] = File(...) makes the handler call request.form() before screen_human runs; Starlette streams the whole multipart body and rolls every file part past the 1 MiB spool threshold into a SpooledTemporaryFile under the control plane's TMPDIR.

trace.scope: per-file cap applied after parsing and after authentication
trace.description: limit = settings.max_upload_bytes with await f.read(limit + 1) at 281-283 executes only inside the endpoint, i.e. after the whole body has been spooled and only when a principal was already accepted, so it cannot bound pre-auth work.

trace.scope: the only middleware installed on the app (no body-size gate on the way into FastAPI's body stage)
trace.description: _NoFraming is the last app-owned code a request passes, and it only appends response headers. With cli.py:127 and deploy/Caddyfile:5 adding no limit either, the attacker-chosen body becomes control-plane heap and temp-disk state before principal()/screen_human can reject it.

evidence.description: _NoFraming (63-80), registered at 113, is the app's only middleware: app.add_middleware appears exactly once in the tree, so there is no body-limit middleware.
reverse_proxy agentbox:8765 with no request_body directive: the shipped proxy forwards request bodies without a size bound.
The only upload bound is max_upload_bytes (50 MiB per file by default); it is consumed inside the endpoint at api.py:278-283, after parsing and after authentication.
LOGGED_ARGS_MAX / LOGGED_ARGS_HEAD (37-38) cap only the audit copy of tool args, after a principal is established.
The compose deployment runs the single agentbox service behind Caddy with AGENTBOX_BEHIND_TLS_PROXY=1, no mem_limit and no request-size limit, exposing 8765 only on the compose network.

CMD agentbox serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765 --behind-tls-proxy: the one uvicorn process (cli.py:127) serves the JSON API, the approval UI and the audit chain, so buffered bytes hit shared availability rather than one isolated worker.

conditions.description: None: no Authorization header and no session cookie are required for the buffering; every tested path returned 401 only after the body had been consumed.
The client can reach the control plane through the shipped Caddy front end (compose publishes 443/80 and forwards bodies without a size directive), or directly when agentbox serve is used.

Impact scales with the memory and TMPDIR of the single uvicorn process that also serves the human approval queue and the audit chain; the compose service sets no mem_limit, so exhausting the process takes the approval path down with it (pending approvals, 300 s default, age toward timeout while the operator restarts).

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated network client that never holds a token sends bodies of its choosing to routes it knows will answer 401, or to the upload route, and lets the control plane read, decode and spool them. The attacker's spend is the bytes it uploads, while the server retains about twice that in heap per in-flight body (measured), with no per-request and no concurrency bound in the shipped configuration.
payloads:
POST /sandboxes HTTP/1.1
Host: agentbox.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 16777216

{"source_dir": null, "template": "cli", "pad": "AAAA..."}

POST /sandboxes/sid1/files HTTP/1.1
Host: agentbox.example.com
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=X-BOUNDARY

--X-BOUNDARY
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="files"; filename="a.bin"
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

<4194304 bytes>
--X-BOUNDARY--
instructions: Inside the approved OS sandbox only (no network, no Docker socket, 512 MiB, 1 CPU, uid 65534, 120 s), with /target read-only on PYTHONPATH and AGENTBOX_HOME under /scratch: replace docker.from_env with an in-process fake whose info() reports only the runc runtime, then build the real app with api.build(Settings()) from the audited tree.

Drive the app at the ASGI layer with an HTTP scope for the target path and a receive() that streams the declared body in 64 KiB http.request messages, recording how many body bytes the app consumed before it emitted http.response.start.

Patch starlette.requests.Request.json to record len(raw body) at decode time, and starlette.formparsers.SpooledTemporaryFile to record max_size, bytes written, whether it rolled to a real temporary file and that file's on-disk size under TMPDIR.

Send the payloads with no Authorization header and no cookie; record the status, the bytes consumed before the response started, and the decode/spool records. Read resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss before and after the largest JSON request to bound the memory effect. Keep the largest body at 16 MiB so the sandbox limit is never approached, and stop after the first confirming observation.
Send a control request (GET /healthz, no body) through the same driver to prove the app object is functional and the 401 comes from the credential check.
execution.observed_result: Installed stack: fastapi 0.161.1, starlette 1.9.0, uvicorn 0.54.0. POST /sandboxes with a 16,777,216-byte JSON body and no Authorization returned 401, but the app had consumed all 16,777,216 bytes before emitting http.response.start and Request.json() had decoded 16,777,216 bytes; peak RSS grew 32,768 KiB (2.0x the body). /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/exec, /sandboxes/{sid}/restore and /approvals/{aid} behaved identically with 4,194,304-byte bodies - all bytes consumed and decoded before the 401. POST /sandboxes/{sid}/files with one 4,194,304-byte part and no cookie returned 401 after consuming all 4,194,442 bytes; at that moment the SpooledTemporaryFile (max_size 1,048,576) had rolled to a real temporary file holding 4,194,184 bytes in TMPDIR, the endpoint's 50 MiB per-file cap never ran, and the temporary file was removed when the form closed (no residue afterwards). A control GET /healthz returned 200 with 0 body bytes consumed. The installed multipart parser carries max_files/max_fields = 1000 and max_part_size = 1 MiB, but max_part_size is applied only to non-file fields, so a 4 MiB file part passed untouched.

remediation.strategy: Reject oversized bodies before FastAPI's body stage and before any authentication work: install an ASGI middleware beside _NoFraming that answers 413 when the declared Content-Length already exceeds the cap and counts streamed bytes for chunked bodies, aborting at the cap; keep the application/JSON cap above the largest legitimate body (write_file content is bounded by max_write_bytes = 1 MiB, so a 64 KiB JSON cap would break authenticated tool calls) and give the multipart route an aggregate body cap from a new setting (default e.g. 64 MiB for the whole request, not per file); and add request_body { max_size ... } to deploy/Caddyfile so the shipped proxy refuses the same oversized bodies before they reach the process.

code_changes.fixed_code:
# FastAPI가 본문을 읽기 전에 거부할 요청 본문 상한. write_file 인자(max_write_bytes)보다 커야 한다.
    max_body_bytes: int = field(default_factory=lambda: int(_env("AGENTBOX_MAX_BODY", str(4 * 1024 * 1024))))
    # 업로드 경로의 요청 전체 상한 (파일 하나가 아니라 한 요청)
    max_upload_body_bytes: int = field(
        default_factory=lambda: int(_env("AGENTBOX_MAX_UPLOAD_BODY", str(64 * 1024 * 1024))))

likelihood.reason: No token, no interaction and no knowledge beyond the route list: one ordinary HTTP request whose declared body the attacker chooses, and the same request works on four JSON routes and the upload route.

impact.reason: Availability of the single control-plane process that also serves the human approval queue and the audit chain: memory grows about 2x the bytes sent per request (measured +32 MiB for a 16 MiB body), there is no per-request body cap and no concurrency limit, so retained memory scales with concurrent in-flight bodies; the decode/parse of the buffered body runs in the request task on the event loop, stalling unrelated requests while it works, and the multipart path also writes attacker-sized bytes to the container's TMPDIR. No confidentiality or integrity boundary is crossed, and an operator who adds a proxy body cap or a container mem_limit removes the effect.

confidence.reason: Every cited line exists in the audited tree at 9805d91 (trace and evidence re-read line by line), and an independent ASGI-level reproduction on the real app object with the installed fastapi 0.161.1 / starlette 1.9.0 reproduced the claimed result: the full body was consumed and decoded before the 401, and the multipart part was on disk before the 401. No middleware, uvicorn option or shipped proxy directive bounds the body. The ordering is FastAPI/Starlette default behaviour (calibration only, since the architecture summary names no comparable product baseline); agentbox bounds its other resource paths explicitly (tool_pool, PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX, max_upload_bytes, LOGGED_ARGS_MAX), so this omission is not a deliberate design choice.

title: same_origin compares only the Origin netloc with Host, so an http:// page on the same host passes the CSRF origin check of a TLS deployment and can clear the session cookie
description: Every cookie-authenticated UI mutation funnels through api.same_origin (api.py:131-133), which returns True when Origin is absent or when urlsplit(Origin).netloc equals the Host header; the scheme is never compared. A plaintext http://H page is a different web origin from the TLS deployment https://H but carries the same netloc, so the gate accepts it. Independently reproduced (agents/v02/scratch/v02_origin.py, artifact v02_origin.out; api.build with docker.from_env stubbed, ASGI served as https://agentbox.example): Origin http://agentbox.example was accepted for POST /login (303, issuing the Secure SameSite=strict HttpOnly host-only session cookie), POST /ui/approvals/apr_000000000000/approve (200; box.decide entered with the '*' session and rendered approval-not-found), POST /ui/sandboxes (handler reached box.create_sandbox) and POST /logout (303; end_ui_session entered, server session ended - a later GET /ui with the same cookie redirected to /login). Origin https://agentbox.example was accepted identically; Origin https://evil.example, Origin: null, Origin http://agentbox.example@evil.example and Origin http://agentbox.example:8443 against Host agentbox.example were all 403; a POST with no Origin was accepted. Consequence (1): where a browser attaches the Strict cookie to a cross-scheme POST, the human-scoped action runs - approve/deny for a known apr_ id, a sandbox built for an attacker-chosen source_dir, or server-side session end. Consequence (2), browser-independent once the request is sent: POST /logout answers even a cookieless cross-origin request with 303 plus an unconditional cookie-clearing Set-Cookie (web.py:149-150), so a page served at http://H forces a client-side logout while the server-side session survives. No anti-CSRF token, Referer or Sec-Fetch check exists anywhere in agentbox/ (grep finds none) and the only response-wide guard is X-Object-Frame/CSP frame-ancestors (api.py:66), which stops iframe clickjacking but not a top-level auto-submitted form; no Strict-Transport-Security is emitted in agentbox/ or deploy/ (no response carries one; only audit docs mention it), so nothing forces the upgrade of http://H. The decisive unknown stays the browser's schemeful same-site behaviour: the run-3 loopback Chromium 141 run had the Secure cookie withheld (only the forced browser logout occurred), no browser exists in sbx, and Firefox/WebKit are unobserved, so whether consequence (1) is reachable cannot be decided from source or from this sandbox.
claimed_root_cause: api.py:131-133: same_origin() returns True when urlsplit(origin).netloc == headers.get('host') (and when Origin is absent); the scheme is never compared, and the closure receives only headers (api.py:131) although the app derives the request scheme elsewhere (api.py:136, web.py:114). Nothing in agentbox/ or deploy/ emits Strict-Transport-Security (deploy/Caddyfile:5 is a bare reverse_proxy), so the CSRF gate degrades to whatever same-site semantics the browser applies to http://H versus https://H.

trace.scope: decide - POST /ui/approvals/{aid}/{decision} (peers: create web.py:174, logout web.py:142)
trace.description: Cookie-authenticated, form-encodable mutations with no anti-CSRF token; the only origin binding is same_origin. All three decorators verified in the audited tree.

Resolves the browser cookie via box.desktop.session_scope() at api.py:142 and then calls same_origin(request.headers) at api.py:145; logout calls the same closure directly at web.py:144. The cookie is checked before the origin, so a cross-scheme request without a cookie gets 401 rather than 403.

Netloc-only comparison, missing Origin accepted - reproduced: Origin http://agentbox.example passes against a request served over https://agentbox.example, foreign host, null, the userinfo trick and a port mismatch fail.

With the request accepted the human-scoped action runs: decide executes the stored args with actor='human' and the '*' session, create builds a sandbox for a form-supplied source_dir, and logout ends the session when the cookie did arrive.

evidence.description: urlsplit(origin).netloc == headers.get('host') drops the scheme component, so http://H and https://H are indistinguishable to the gate; reproduced accepting http://agentbox.example for a request served as https://agentbox.example.

same_origin is typed to receive only headers, so the served scheme is not even in scope; the app already derives it from request.url.scheme at api.py:136 and web.py:114, which is the seam a fix needs.

set_cookie issues the session cookie httponly=True, samesite='strict', max_age=12h, host-only (no Domain); observed Set-Cookie: HttpOnly; Max-Age=43200; Path=/; SameSite=strict; Secure under the https fixture. Whether it travels on a cross-scheme POST is browser policy (schemeful same-site), the decisive unknown.

logout builds a 303 and calls r.delete_cookie(D.COOKIE) unconditionally at web.py:150, even when end_ui_session returned None because no cookie was attached; reproduced: cookieless cross-scheme POST /logout -> 303 with agentbox_session cleared (Max-Age=0, Path=/) while the server session state is untouched.

s.secure_cookie = s.secure_cookie or tls or behind: the Secure attribute is forced exactly for direct-TLS and behind-TLS-proxy deployments, i.e. the deployments where the http/https scheme fork exists.

The only response-wide middleware adds X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN and CSP frame-ancestors 'self'; there is no CSRF token, Referer or Sec-Fetch-Site validation in agentbox/ (grep over *.py finds none) and no TrustedHostMiddleware, so a top-level form POST is unguarded beyond same_origin.

The site block is a bare reverse_proxy agentbox:8765; no header directive, no HSTS anywhere in deploy/, agentbox/ or images/ (tree-wide grep for Strict-Transport-Security matches only audit docs), and the fixture responses carry no strict-transport-security header.

Behind-proxy mode trusts X-Forwarded-Proto (proxy_headers=True, forwarded_allow_ips from AGENTBOX_TRUSTED_PROXIES) and deploy/Caddyfile:2-3 says the proxy supplies Host and X-Forwarded-Proto, so request.url.scheme is a usable served scheme for the regression fix.

Verifier's own ASGI reproduction (produced in sbx from agents/v02/scratch/v02_origin.py; session ids redacted): cross-scheme Origin accepted on /login, /ui/approvals approve and /ui/sandboxes, 403 for foreign/null/userinfo/port-mismatch, 303 plus clearing Set-Cookie on /logout both with and without a cookie, and no HSTS on any response.

Real Chromium 141, run-3 parent-live (not re-run here): the cross-scheme POST had same_origin accept the http Origin but the Secure SameSite=Strict cookie was withheld (schemeful same-site), so only delete_cookie forced a client-side logout; the server session was not ended. Firefox and WebKit are unobserved.

blockers: Browser behaviour (decisive): whether a browser an operator actually uses attaches the Secure SameSite=strict session cookie to a cross-scheme http://H -> https://H form POST. Chromium 141 withheld it (docs/security-audit/run-3/agents/parent-live/artifacts/l3/l4.out:4, reported, not re-run in run-4); Firefox and WebKit current behaviour and the legacy cut-offs are untested, no browser exists in sbx, and the answer cannot be derived from source. Without the cookie only consequence (2), the client-side forced logout, remains.

Network position: whether an attacker can serve plaintext http://H on the deployment host name at all (on-path network attacker, a plaintext listener on port 80, or a DNS/HTTP hijack). No Strict-Transport-Security is emitted anywhere in agentbox/ or deploy/, so nothing forces the upgrade, but whether an on-path attacker and browser preload state are in scope is an owner decision.

Deployment shape: whether both schemes are exposed at the same effective netloc (direct TLS on 443 plus cleartext 80, or behind-proxy mode where Caddy owns the http->https redirect). In a loopback http-only deployment the scheme fork does not exist, and if HSTS or a preload entry is present the http page never loads.

validation_plan.local: Repo-side half is done and reproduced by the verifier: agents/v02/scratch/v02_origin.py builds the real app (api.build with docker.from_env stubbed) and drives it over ASGI as https://agentbox.example - cross-scheme Origin accepted on /login, /ui/approvals approve, /ui/sandboxes and /logout, foreign/null/userinfo/port-mismatch 403, /logout always emitting the clearing Set-Cookie; artifact v02_origin.out. Remaining decisive step is a loopback browser lab run outside sbx (parent-live): map H to 127.0.0.1, start agentbox with --tls-cert/--tls-key (self-signed, lab-trusted) on https://H:443 with a dummy human token, and a plaintext http://H:80 page that auto-submits a top-level form to https://H/logout and to https://H/ui/sandboxes with source_dir set; log in on https://H, open http://H, and record (a) whether agentbox_session is sent on the POST, (b) whether the response is 303/200 (accepted) rather than 403, (c) for /logout whether the server session ends (GET /ui then 303 /login) and whether a ui_logout row appears in /audit, (d) for /ui/sandboxes whether a new sandbox exists. Repeat on current Firefox and WebKit and on any engine or policy that disables schemeful same-site. Regression: change same_origin to compare BOTH the scheme and the netloc, taking the served scheme from request.url.scheme (already used at api.py:136 and web.py:114, and X-Forwarded-Proto-aware under cli.py:126) instead of the headers-only signature at api.py:131; then both cross-scheme POSTs must return 403 and the clearing Set-Cookie must disappear, while Origin https://H with Host H still passes and the existing tests/test_unit.py suite stays green.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner confirms, without probing live endpoints: (1) whether the operator-facing host name sends Strict-Transport-Security or is on the browser preload list; (2) whether a plaintext http:// listener for that name is reachable (direct TLS on 443 plus cleartext 80, or a TLS proxy fronting the plaintext port where the http->https redirect is the only barrier) and whether an on-path attacker is in scope; (3) which browser engines and versions operators use; (4) whether any operator browser or policy lacks schemeful same-site. If HSTS is present and every browser is schemeful, only the browser-independent forced-logout residual from the unconditional delete_cookie at web.py:149-150 remains, and the same scheme comparison removes it.

title: Agent-grown audit and approval rows in the shared control-plane SQLite file have no aggregate bound or retention, so an agent can fill the host disk and neither recovery path keeps the audit chain
description: Every accepted agent tool request appends two audit rows (tool_request before the policy decision, policy_decision as soon as decide() returns) before any approval request, snapshot or execution, a risky call adds an approval_requested row plus an approvals row holding the full raw args, and every failed POST /approvals/{aid} adds an approval_forbidden row. Args are now capped per record (80,000-byte command is stored as a 16,384-byte head), but nothing bounds the tables: in an isolated fixture two rows per call added 17,203 bytes to the .db file, identically at n=20 and n=40, and 512 bytes per call for {command: ls}; five approval rows of 400,000-byte args took 2,007,040 bytes and every row survived executed/denied/expired. Triggers abort UPDATE and DELETE on audit, grep finds no DELETE for audit or approvals, no VACUUM, no count/size quota and no retention job, so growth is permanent and host disk is the only limit. When the volume fills, AuditLog.append raises AuditWriteError, which service.py turns into 503 for tool calls, human lifecycle, approval decisions and handbacks, so all sandboxes stop rather than the offending one. Recovery is not available either: deleting the oldest rows made verify() fail permanently at the first survivor (broken_at=7, 'id가 1 다음에 7로 건너뜀'), while deleting every row made verify() report ok=True with checked=0, so an operator must choose between permanently broken verification and a silently erased history.
claimed_root_cause: The audit table is append-only by design (audit.py:35-38) and the per-record arg cap (service.py:37-38, 180-194) is the only bound on agent-driven growth; grep over agentbox/ finds no aggregate quota, retention window, pruning command or size check for the audit or approvals tables (the only sqlite DELETEs are ui_tickets, ui_sessions and takeover_leases in desktop.py), and the delete path for a sandbox only unlinks capture PNGs (service.py:106-109, 471-475). The shared SQLite file used by AuditLog, SandboxManager, ApprovalStore and DesktopControl (api.py:86-94, config.py:84-86, default ./data/agentbox.db, host bind mount at deploy/docker-compose.yml:28) therefore has the host volume as its only limit, and capacity recovery is mutually exclusive with the integrity contract (audit.py:230-236).

trace.description: An agent token reaches this route through principal() (api.py:115-124). The body is ToolCall whose args is an unconstrained dict[str, Any] (api.py:51-52), and there is no request-body, key-count or value-size cap on this route; the only body cap in the API is the human upload route (api.py:278-283) and the shipped Caddyfile is a bare reverse_proxy with no request_body limit (deploy/Caddyfile:4-6).

tool_request is appended with _logged_args(args) (295-296) and policy_decision is appended the moment policy.decide returns (297, appended at 303), before any approval request (324), snapshot (343) or execution, so every accepted request writes two rows even when the decision is DENY (308-309) and nothing runs.

Only the single record is bounded: args over 64 KiB become a 16 KiB head plus args_bytes and args_sha256. Measured: {'command': 'a'*80000} produced args_head of exactly 16,384 bytes and args_bytes 80,015; the two rows added 17,203 bytes per call at both n=20 and n=40 (linear), and {command: 'ls'} added 512 bytes per call, so per-record capping does not bound the table.

approvals.create stores the full raw args and preview with no cap (approvals.py:49-59); PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX=20 (service.py:44, 312-316) limits pending concurrency only, and measured rows of 400,000-byte args took 401,408 bytes each and were still present after executed, denied and expired transitions. A sandbox delete does not remove them.

The row is inserted into the same SQLite file; the append-only triggers (audit.py:35-38) abort any UPDATE and DELETE (both reproduced: 'audit log is append-only'), and no code path in the package removes audit rows.

At disk-full every append raises AuditWriteError, which becomes ServiceError(503) here (593-594) and likewise for tool calls (305-306), approval decisions (402-404) and handbacks (539-541), so the blast radius is every sandbox and every human operation rather than the agent's own process.

verify starts from GENESIS with expected_id 1 and rejects the first row that does not chain (233-236). Reclaiming space by deleting the oldest rows therefore fails permanently (measured: after removing ids 1..6, ok=False, broken_at=7), while deleting every row returns ok=True with checked=0, so capacity recovery either breaks /audit/verify for good or erases the history without a trace.

evidence.description: audit_no_update and audit_no_delete raise ABORT 'audit log is append-only'; the fixture reproduced both rejections.
verify() rejects any row whose id is not expected_id and any prev_hash that does not match, which is what makes prefix pruning distinguishable from tampering forever.
LOGGED_ARGS_MAX and LOGGED_ARGS_HEAD are the only size controls on the audit path and they are per record, not per table, per sandbox or per deployment.
The author comment states the audit log cannot be deleted and that an agent growing it with large args cannot be undone.

drop_captures removes only capture PNGs (106-109) and delete_sandbox only calls it (471-475); approval rows holding the full unmasked args and preview survive decision and expiry (5 of 5 measured rows remained) and nothing removes them on sandbox deletion.

snapshot_quota exists specifically so an agent cannot fill host disk with docker commits without a human, showing the intended invariant that agent actions are host-disk bounded; no comparable control exists for the audit or approvals tables.
create() stores json.dumps(args) and the preview with no cap, and ApprovalStore exposes no delete method; 400,000-byte args measured 401,408 bytes per row.

AuditLog, SandboxManager, ApprovalStore and DesktopControl all open settings.db_path, so one file carries all four components' state (config.py:84-86; the compose deployment bind-mounts that home on the host, deploy/docker-compose.yml:28).

/ui/approvals loads every historical approval row for the sandbox with full args and preview parsed and then keeps the last five (208-209); agentbox/templates/index.html:25 and agentbox/templates/sandbox.html:25 poll that view every 2 s, so retained rows keep costing control-plane read work.

blockers: Free space, any filesystem or volume quota, and the planned lifetime of the volume holding data/agentbox.db (config.py:29 home=./data, config.py:84-86 db_path, deployed as a host bind mount at deploy/docker-compose.yml:26-28) are deployment facts. Nothing in the repository bounds stored total: no retention, no count or size quota, no VACUUM. At the measured 17,203 bytes per maximum-size tool call (512 bytes for a trivial call) the time to exhaustion depends entirely on that free space, from minutes on a small volume to months on a large one, and no repository fact decides it.

The call rate an agent can sustain is partly a deployment fact: the repository has no rate limit on the tool route, tool_concurrency=4 (config.py:53) and the 32-thread tool_pool (api.py:103) bound concurrency only, and the shipped Caddyfile is a bare reverse_proxy (deploy/Caddyfile:4-6), but any operator-added proxy or network control is outside the source.

Whether operators prune or rotate that SQLite file out of band, and which loss they accept, is a deployment/owner decision: source and fixture show that partial pruning permanently fails /audit/verify (audit.py:230-236) while total truncation passes as an empty log, so the product offers no capacity recovery that keeps the history verifiable.

validation_plan.local: Already performed in the approved sandbox (tools/sbx.py v03: /target read-only on PYTHONPATH, /scratch writable, no network, no Docker socket, uid 65534, 512 MiB, 120 s). Built AuditLog and ApprovalStore on scratch databases and replayed exactly what _call_tool writes: (1) _logged_args('exec', {'command': 'a'*80000}) returned args_head of 16,384 bytes and args_bytes 80,015; (2) 20 and 40 pairs of tool_request plus policy_decision rows added 344,064 and 688,128 bytes after PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE), i.e. 17,203 bytes per call at both sizes, and 40 pairs with {'command': 'ls'} added 20,480 bytes, i.e. 512 bytes per call; (3) DELETE FROM audit and UPDATE audit both failed with sqlite3.IntegrityError 'audit log is append-only'; (4) dropping only the delete trigger and removing ids 1..6 left verify() returning ok=False, checked=0, broken_at=7, reason 'id가 1 다음에 7로 건너뜀', while deleting every row left verify() returning ok=True with checked=0; (5) five ApprovalStore rows of 400,000-byte args took 2,007,040 bytes (401,408 each) and all five were still listed after executed, denied and expired, with no delete method on the store; (6) approvals.list() re-parses full args. The disk-full to AuditWriteError to 503 conversion was not exercised (filling a filesystem is a saturation test); it rests on audit.py:193-194 wrapping sqlite3.Error and the fail-closed handlers cited in the trace. Output: scratch/fixout.txt and scratch/fixout2.txt; the numbers above were observed directly, the files are supplementary.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a throwaway deployment, never a shared or production host, and without filling the volume: record the free space and any quota on the volume holding data/agentbox.db; issue 200 bounded tool calls from one agent token with 80,000-byte exec commands (denied calls are sufficient, since the two audit rows are written before any execution) and 200 with {command: ls}; confirm the .db size delta is about 3.4 MB and 0.1 MB respectively and that it does not shrink after the calls stop, after sandbox deletion, or after any documented maintenance command; then check whether the operator has any out-of-band retention or rotation for that file, and confirm that once the volume is full the tool route and the human lifecycle route both return 503 from AuditWriteError while other sandboxes are unaffected by definition only. Extrapolate from the per-call delta instead of filling the disk.

title: list_dir, outbox_list, preview glob expansion and screenshot buffer unbounded container output in the shared control-plane process
description: On a sandbox that the agent token controls, four control-plane readers take the whole container-produced stream through Docker's non-streaming exec_run, with no byte cap and, for three of them, no container-side timeout: SandboxManager.list_dir (sandbox.py:428) runs `ls -la` on any /workspace or /source path; SandboxManager.outbox_list (sandbox.py:534) runs an unbounded `find -maxdepth 1 -printf`; SandboxManager._expand (sandbox.py:560) globs a preview pattern; DesktopTools.screenshot (sandbox_desktop.py:86-88) `cat`s /home/desktop/.cache/agentbox-shot.png and only then checks the PNG magic. _truncate (sandbox_common.py:24-32) and _parse_outbox (sandbox.py:111-124) run after the whole buffer exists, so they bound the returned value, not the peak. The peak is paid by the one shared FastAPI process, so one sandbox's listing is charged to every sandbox. Measured locally against the real reader functions with a fake exec_run: a 16 MiB stream makes list_dir peak at 16.19 MiB, against 0.32 MiB for exec's _Head reader on the same stream; 5.0 MB of find output becomes 58.6 MiB retained and 72.6 MiB peak after _parse_outbox (12.3x, record count uncapped); 4.2 MB of glob output becomes 209,715 Python strings; an 8 MiB PNG is accepted unchanged and then base64-encoded to 11.2 MB for the agent response (service.py:143). The screenshot path is the one with superlinear amplitude: the shot file sits in the desktop user's writable home (_SHOT, sandbox_desktop.py:32), so uid 1001 can point it at a character device and turn one cheap call into up to 15 s of unthrottled `cat`, bounded only by a wall clock (_X_TIMEOUT, sandbox_desktop.py:26,46-50), whose exit-code check also runs after the read. The host-disk half of the claim is narrower than proposed: service.py:328 writes the captured PNG with no size check, but only after the magic test passes, so a /dev/zero symlink costs memory and no disk; a huge PNG-prefixed file is needed for the disk variant. The list_dir/outbox_list/_expand variants are ~1:1 with container output, and the container's output ceiling is its writable layer, which the repository caps only when the optional AGENTBOX_DISK is set (config.py:42, sandbox.py:263-264).
claimed_root_cause: The _Head/_OUT_LIMIT discipline for exec and the container-side _timed plus head -c discipline for read_file, outbox_read and workspace_manifest were applied reader by reader; four readers that consume attacker-selected container output were left with a plain exec_run read (sandbox.py:428, 534, 560 and sandbox_desktop.py:86-88), and the screenshot reader's only bound is a timeout that is checked after the full read.

trace.description: Agent-token route for the sandbox's own tools. default_policy.yaml:10 is `default: allow`, so list_dir and screenshot reach the readers below with no approval and no snapshot.
Runs on a tool_pool thread; the reader work and its peak memory happen on that shared pool, outside any per-call size accounting.
Returns sb.list_dir(sid, path) straight into the tool result with no byte, entry or time check on the way.
Calls sb.screenshot and then base64-encodes the entire PNG into the tool response at 143, so the response holds a second full copy of container-controlled bytes.

The exec preview is computed before the approval row exists, so sandboxes.preview -> _expand streams glob output even if the human then denies, and once per pending request (up to PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX).
The whole ls stream is read into the control plane with no byte cap and no container-side timeout; _truncate at 432 shortens the value only after the peak has been allocated.
Shell glob output is buffered whole, then decoded and returned as one string per match; the caller materialises the entire list into preview notes.

find -printf output is buffered whole and parsed afterwards into one dict per record, then sorted, with no count cap; reached from the human routes api.py:290 and web.py:233, where container-chosen names drive the cost.
`cat {_SHOT}` (86) is buffered completely, bounded only by the 15 s timeout, and the PNG magic plus exit-code checks run at 89 only after the full read.

evidence.description: _Head.add keeps only _OUT_LIMIT+1 bytes and merely counts the remainder; only exec's reader (411-416) uses it for container output.

exec streams with api.exec_start(..., stream=True, demux=True), and the comment at 408-409 names the exact hazard (a single cat /dev/zero buffering hundreds of MB). This is the control the four readers skip.
list_dir exec_run with no _timed wrapper and no head -c; the argv captured locally is ['ls','-la','--','/workspace'] with kwargs demux/user/workdir only.
_truncate(out) runs after the whole stream is in memory, so the 64 KiB listing is a display cap, not a memory cap.
read_file does use _timed(_READ_TIMEOUT, ...) plus head -c limit+1, i.e. the sibling that got both guards.
workspace_manifest does use _timed(_MANIFEST_TIMEOUT, ...) plus `| head -c _MANIFEST_CAP` at 378.
outbox_read does use _timed(_READ_TIMEOUT, ...) plus head -c limit+1.
_parse_outbox builds one dict per NUL record, sorts the list and applies no count cap: locally 5.0 MB of records became 58.6 MiB retained.
_expand decodes the whole stream and returns every match line; 4.2 MB of output became 209,715 strings.
_X_TIMEOUT = 15 is the only bound on the screenshot exec; there is no byte cap anywhere on this path.
_SHOT is /home/desktop/.cache/agentbox-shot.png, inside the desktop user's own home, so uid 1001 can replace it with a symlink before the control plane cats it.
_x raises on exit 124/137 only after exec_run returned, i.e. after the full read; the timeout bounds wall clock, not bytes already buffered.
The screenshot result is base64-encoded into the tool response: +33% bytes and a second simultaneous copy of the PNG.
In the approval path the same PNG is written to settings.home/captures with no size check; it is only reached when the PNG magic check at sandbox_desktop.py:89 passes.
_summary drops 'listing' from the audit row for list_dir, so the audit log is not the amplifier on this path (calibration against the unbounded-args finding).
outbox_list's own entrypoint is the human screen route (web.py:233 for the UI fragment), not the agent tool route in the trace.
disk_limit defaults to empty and sandbox.py:263-264 sets storage_opt only when it is non-empty, so by default the container side of the 1:1 readers is bounded only by the host disk.

blockers: The decisive quantity - how much memory the control plane actually holds while a real container streams - is produced inside the docker SDK's non-streaming exec_start reader. The approved sandbox has no Docker daemon or socket (uid 65534, no /var/run/docker.sock), so no real exec stream can be created or sized; the peaks reported here come from an in-process fake exec_run that hands the real reader functions pre-built bytes, which understates the real peak because the SDK buffers the same bytes as well.

The superlinear variant needs /home/desktop/.cache/agentbox-shot.png replaced by a symlink to /dev/zero (or to a huge PNG-prefixed file) by uid 1001 inside a live agentbox-desktop sandbox; the audit sandbox has neither that image nor an X session, and the control plane's own `scrot -o -z` overwrites the path on the non-symlink case.

Whether the resulting peak is fatal depends on owner-side topology that the repository does not fix: deploy/ sets no memory limit for the agentbox service, the host's memory and any cgroup limit are unknown, AGENTBOX_DISK is unset by default, and the blast radius (control-plane restart drops every sandbox's desktop session and in-flight approvals) is an operational fact.

validation_plan.local: Owner-run on a disposable Docker-backed sandbox with AGENTBOX_DISK=2g and no network. (1) Create ~200k empty files in /workspace using unapproved batch `touch` calls (touch is in the read-only allowlist, default_policy.yaml:25-27) or one gated exec. (2) Record VmHWM from /proc/<pid>/status of the control-plane process, call POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/list_dir {"path":"/workspace"} with a dummy agent token, record VmHWM again, and confirm the returned listing stops at 64 KiB while the peak grew by roughly the raw ls size. (3) Control: run the same directory through the capped exec reader (`ls -la /workspace`) and confirm the delta stays near 64 KiB. (4) Put 200k files in /workspace/outbox, call GET /sandboxes/{sid}/outbox, and check for the ~12x parse amplification measured here. (5) Send one `rm /workspace/*` exec so the REQUIRE_APPROVAL branch runs _preview before any human decision, and measure the _expand cost. (6) Desktop variant: in a disposable desktop sandbox, as uid 1001 point the shot path at /dev/zero, call POST /tools/screenshot, and stop the test as soon as VmHWM growth is visible, noting whether the 15 s timeout keeps it under the host limit.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on the compose stack: watch the agentbox container's RSS while a dummy agent lists a 200k-entry /workspace, compare it with the same agent running an allowlisted `ls -la` through the capped exec reader, and record whether the service has a cgroup memory limit and what an OOM does to running sandboxes and pending approvals. Then, with captures enabled, watch the same RSS during a burst of gated calls against a desktop sandbox whose shot path was replaced by a device symlink, and confirm that no file appears under settings.home/captures in the /dev/zero case while a huge PNG-prefixed file does produce one.

title: GUI burst stray kill spares a uid-1001 process in a burst-start session whose pid the client-declared _NET_WM_PID window list names
description: Verified in the audited tree (9805d91): at GUI-burst close GuiBursts._finish (gui_bursts.py:120) calls _stop_strays, which reads desktop_processes (gui_bursts.py:83) and kills gui_strays(procs, wins, burst['pids']) (gui_bursts.py:84-85). For a new uid-1001 process the only remaining exemption is the window test: p['pid'] in window_pids or a non-baseline ancestor pid in window_pids (gui_state.py:85-86); baseline pids, pid 1, other uids and docker-exec roots are exempted earlier (gui_state.py:80). window_pids are the decimal tokens of `xdotool getwindowpid` over `xdotool search --onlyvisible --name .` (sandbox_desktop.py:59-61), i.e. the _NET_WM_PID property the X client writes for itself; the parser filters with isdigit only, never checks that the pid owns a window or is the declaring client, and xdotool is run as the desktop account on the desktop-owned display (sandbox_desktop.py:46-47, images/desktop/agentbox-desktop-start:20,30,38). I re-ran the real gui_state.gui_strays and the real GuiBursts._stop_strays in the sandbox (agents/v05/artifacts/v05_probe.out): a headless uid-1001 daemon 300 in the burst-start session sid 1, parented by the baseline Thunar 85, is killed when window_pids is empty (line 2) and is spared when the window list merely names 300 (line 3); naming an unrelated pid 301 does not spare it (line 4), and a windowed but baseline ancestor 85 does not spare it (line 5). With the real _stop_strays the forged case killed nothing and emitted no gui_processes_stopped record at all, while the control case killed [300] and logged it (lines 20-22). Two preconditions bound the claim, and both are runtime facts of the image rather than source facts. (1) The window test is reached only when p['sid'] is in base_sids, the sessions of the uid-1001 baseline pids (gui_state.py:63,82-84); a new session is killed regardless of window, which my run confirms for a daemon in sid 777 (line 8). tests/test_unit.py:330-334 encodes exactly that for a terminal opened during a burst: the terminal window 150 is spared but its shell 152 and the shell's job 160 are killed as a new session, so a daemon typed into a terminal opened during the burst is not in this candidate's class. (2) The attacker needs an X client that can set _NET_WM_PID to another process's pid and then have xdotool report it; the image recipe installs xdotool, socat and x11-xserver-utils but not x11-utils (xprop), python or a compiler (images/desktop/Dockerfile:17-23), so whether such a client exists in the running image is unobserved. Impact is bounded and detective-control shaped: GUI input is approval-free by design (N-1) and the burst's snapshot and gui_changes are its documented record. A spared daemon keeps writing /workspace after the close, where the only manifest read (gui_bursts.py:122) has already happened, and its writes produce no gui_changes and no gui_processes_stopped row; because it is then present at the next burst open (gui_bursts.py:70,76), gui_state.py:80 treats it as baseline forever, which is the candidate's 'survives every burst close'. Calibration, not dismissal: the by-design ancestor clause already spares a helper of any windowed app opened during the burst (tests/test_unit.py:335-336; my line 9), so the forgery route adds capability mainly for a process with no new windowed ancestor, for example one started from a baseline windowed app such as the pre-existing file manager (tests/test_unit.py:337 keeps such a script in the kill list).
claimed_root_cause: The stray-kill exemption is decided from container-declared X window metadata instead of a control-plane-verifiable link. sandbox_desktop.desktop_processes (sandbox_desktop.py:59-61) turns every decimal token printed by xdotool getwindowpid into a window pid, gui_state.gui_strays (gui_state.py:85-86) spares a new uid-1001 process in a burst-start session when its pid, or a new ancestor pid, is in that set, and gui_bursts._stop_strays (gui_bursts.py:83-85) kills only the remaining pids. Because _NET_WM_PID is written by the X client and every process in the desktop session can reach display :0 (images/desktop/agentbox-desktop-start:20,30,38), the attacker chooses which of its base-session processes look windowed, so the burst-end kill no longer bounds what keeps running.

trace.description: Agent token (lowest-trust network principal, prompt-injectable) posts a GUI input tool. GUI tools are in the allowed set with no approval (service.py:135-139), and GUI input executes as uid 1001 in the desktop session (sandbox_desktop.py:94-129).
For GUI input _needs_snapshot is true, so _snapshot (250-265) takes the recovery snapshot and opens the burst, whose baseline is the workspace manifest plus the current pid set (gui_bursts.py:65-77).

The typed command is delivered into the desktop session as uid 1001. Whether the resulting shell or daemon ends up in a session that existed at burst open is a runtime fact of the image's terminal/launcher behaviour (tests/test_unit.py:330-334 models a terminal shell as a new session that is killed), not a source fact.
When the burst closes (close_idle, gui_bursts.py:137-155) the strays are collected and killed (120) before the closing manifest is read (122).

window_pids is the isdigit-filtered set of xdotool getwindowpid values for every visible window with a non-empty name, i.e. client-declared _NET_WM_PID integers; no window ownership or declaring-client identity is checked (59-61).
A new uid-1001 process in a burst-start session is spared when its pid is in window_pids, or when a non-baseline ancestor pid is, regardless of which process actually owns that window.

kill_processes receives only the unexempted pids (kill -KILL -- <pids> as the desktop account, sandbox_desktop.py:64-67), so a forged-window daemon is not signalled and keeps modifying /workspace after the close.

evidence.description: The windowed test reads only window_pids (client-declared) plus a new-windowed-ancestor heuristic; nothing binds the spared pid to the window's owning client.
The other exemptions are baseline pids, pid 1, non-1001 uids and from_exec (docker-exec roots), so for a base-session process the window test is the sole gate.
base_sids is built only from the sessions of uid-1001 baseline pids, which is why the candidate's class is base-session processes.
A process in a session that did not exist at burst open is killed regardless of any window, bounding the attack to base sessions.
The docstring states the window set is the _NET_WM_PID of visible windows, a property the X client writes.
The xdotool search --onlyvisible --name . / getwindowpid pipeline is run as the desktop account, so any uid-1001 client's windows are in scope.
Output is split and filtered by isdigit only; nothing checks that the pid exists, owns a window, or is the declaring client, and the set is not intersected with procs.
kill_processes signals only the pids it is given, as the desktop account; there is no cgroup or session-wide sweep elsewhere (kill_processes has no other caller).
The stated purpose of the kill is to stop GUI-launched background work that would otherwise keep changing files outside policy after the burst ends.
Only the selected pids are logged as gui_processes_stopped, so a spared daemon leaves no failure record; my run shows the forged case logs nothing and the control logs the kill.
The closing manifest is read after the kill, and nothing reads /workspace again between bursts, so a survivor's later writes are never diffed.
Xvfb, the Xfce session and every GUI tool run as the desktop account via setpriv (19-23, 30, 38), so the display is reachable by uid-1001 code in that session.
startxfce4 runs as the desktop account, the identity the agent's typed GUI input inherits.

Installed packages are xvfb, xauth, x11vnc, socat, xdotool, scrot, x11-xserver-utils, Xfce, thunar, xfce4-terminal, mousepad, procps and base tools; there is no x11-utils (xprop), no python and no compiler, so whether the image can set an arbitrary _NET_WM_PID at all is a runtime fact.
The intended-behaviour test models the shell and job inside a burst-opened terminal as a new session (152) and keeps them in the kill list, which is the precondition this candidate needs to overcome.

My local run of the real gui_strays: with window_pids={300} the headless base-session daemon 300 is absent from the kill list; with the list naming 301 (line 4) or only the baseline ancestor 85 (line 5) it is killed.

blockers: The decisive platform step is not observable here: this sandbox has no X server and no X client. Reproduced in the run (agents/v05/artifacts/v05_probe.out:25-33): DISPLAY unset, /tmp/.X11-unix absent, xdotool/xprop/Xvfb absent, python Xlib absent. So neither 'a uid-1001 client sets _NET_WM_PID to another process's pid' nor 'xdotool getwindowpid reports that value for its window' can be observed.

Related image fact: the recipe (images/desktop/Dockerfile:17-23) provides xdotool and socat but no xprop/x11-utils, no python and no compiler, and xdotool has no generic property setter. Whether the running image contains any program able to write an arbitrary _NET_WM_PID (base-layer or Xfce component, or a hand-written X11-protocol client over the unix socket via socat) must be read from the live image; if none exists the forgery route is refuted for this image and only the by-design ancestor route remains.

Reachability needs the daemon's sid to be one that existed at burst open (gui_state.py:63,82-84): a typed command's shell normally gets a new session (tests/test_unit.py:330-334, my line 8). Whether GUI-only input can place a headless daemon in the startxfce4 session is a runtime property of the image's terminal/launcher behaviour.

Observing survival after a real idle close needs the Docker-backed desktop container (docker exec for ps, xdotool, kill and the audit read); the Docker daemon is forbidden in this verifier sandbox, so the end-to-end kill/no-kill result and the missing gui_processes_stopped row are shown only against the real pure function and the real _stop_strays with a fake container.

validation_plan.local: Disposable agentbox-desktop:0.1 container, network none, built from the audited tree, dummy files only. (1) Record `command -v xprop python3 gcc cc socat xdotool` and `dpkg -l x11-utils` as the property-setter inventory. (2) Start the desktop; as the desktop account via docker exec -u desktop, first start the helper in a burst-start session (launched from the panel/Thunar or from a pre-existing windowed app) and confirm with `ps -eo pid=,ppid=,sid=,uid=,args=` that its sid equals a session that predates the burst; then start the headless writer `sh -c 'while :; do date +%s >> /workspace/_v05_probe; sleep 2; done' &` in that same session. (3) With the inventory from step 1, map a 1x1 titled visible window in that session and set its _NET_WM_PID to the writer's pid (a second window may carry the helper's own pid). If no tool can set the property, stop: the forgery route is refuted for this image. (4) Call the real SandboxManager.desktop_processes(sid) and feed procs/wins into the real gui_state.gui_strays with baseline = the pids taken immediately before step 2; record the wins set and the returned kill list. Expected if the finding holds: the writer pid is absent from the list, while the same call with wins=set() returns it. (5) Call kill_processes(sid, returned list), then confirm by ps that the writer still runs and that /workspace/_v05_probe's mtime advances past AGENTBOX_GUI_SNAPSHOT_IDLE. Non-destructive: dummy probe file only, writer killed and container discarded at the end.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a disposable desktop sandbox with dummy tokens and dummy files: during a real burst drive the agent's click/type to open a terminal from the panel and start `nohup sh -c "while :; do date +%s >> /workspace/_v05_probe; sleep 2; done" &`, plus the property helper if the image has one. Just before close record `ps -eo pid=,ppid=,sid=,uid=,args=` and `for w in $(xdotool search --onlyvisible --name .); do xdotool getwindowpid $w; done`, let the burst close on AGENTBOX_GUI_SNAPSHOT_IDLE, then read GET /audit as the human: the gui_processes_stopped record for that close must omit the writer pid, an exec ps must still show it running, and no later gui_changes row may exist for its writes. Refuted if the writer is killed, or if its session is new so the sid rule kills it, or if the image has no property setter. Fix check: exempt only baseline pids/sessions and control-plane docker-exec ancestry, or bind any spared pid to a control-plane-verified owner (for example the X socket owner in /proc/<pid>/fd) instead of trusting _NET_WM_PID. Audit reads and dummy files only.

title: Approval impact table misreports rm targets whose paths contain whitespace or newlines (an existing file is shown as nonexistent)
description: For a gated exec the "system-computed impact" table is produced by SandboxManager._expand / _walk and preview_command. _expand hands the already-unquoted rm operand to sh as $1 and iterates over $1 unquoted, so the operand is word-split on IFS and each fragment is pathname-expanded before the [ -e ] existence test; results are newline-framed and re-split in Python, and _walk frames find output the same way. preview_command turns an empty match list into "삭제 시도 (현재 존재하지 않음)" and every returned line into a "삭제" row. The rm itself later runs through bash -c with the original quoting, so the computed path set and the executed path set differ: an agent whose workspace target contains a space obtains approval for a deletion the card describes as an apparent no-op, or for a card that lists unrelated decoy files, while the real file is deleted. Reproduced with the verbatim scripts: the card for a lone rm of an existing "final report.docx" showed exactly one row, "삭제 시도 (현재 존재하지 않음)", and no note.
root_cause: The preview path transport is not a lossless representation of a filesystem path. sandbox.py:559 iterates $1 unquoted under the default IFS, so an operand that shlex already unquoted (preview.py:33-44) is re-split into words and each word is expanded again before the existence test; matches are framed with printf "%s\n" and re-split by splitlines() (sandbox.py:562), and _walk's find | head output is split the same way (sandbox.py:565-569). preview.py:90-91 maps an empty expansion to the "does not currently exist" row and preview.py:96-98 maps each returned line to a deletion row, so a split operand both hides the real target and can manufacture paths the command will never touch. The executed command keeps its quoting (sandbox.py:411), so the card and the effect diverge.
intended_behavior: The affected list shown beside the approval must name exactly the paths the stored command will act on, so approving the card is equivalent to approving the effect: a path that exists must never be reported as nonexistent, and a path must never be listed as deleted unless the command deletes it.

trace.description: The agent posts tool=exec with body.args.command under its own sandbox token.
For a REQUIRE_APPROVAL decision (default_policy.yaml:12-16 routes rm to require_approval) the preview is computed while the approval is created, before any human sees it.
exec previews delegate to SandboxManager.preview with the raw command string.
preview_command runs with expand=_expand and walk=_walk bound to the running container.
Each rm operand (quotes already consumed by _split_segments, preview.py:33-44) is expanded once through the container callback.
The operand is passed as $1 and iterated unquoted, so the shell word-splits it on IFS and globs the fragments before [ -e "$p" ]; the surviving words are what get tested.
Matches are framed one per line and re-split with splitlines(), so a name containing a newline arrives as two or more fake paths.
An empty expansion becomes the "삭제 시도 (현재 존재하지 않음)" row and each returned line becomes a deletion row; the result is stored with the approval and rendered as the system-computed impact.

After the human approves, decide() snapshots (service.py:412) and _run_tool passes the stored command unchanged (service.py:126) to exec, which runs it verbatim through bash -c; the quoting is intact there, so the file the table called nonexistent is actually deleted.

evidence.description: for p in $1 - the operand is expanded without quotes under the default IFS, so a space splits it and each fragment is globbed; reproduced with only the cd target retargeted.
An empty match list becomes the "삭제 시도 (현재 존재하지 않음)" row - the false no-op statement for an existing but split path, produced with notes=[].
Matched paths become "삭제" rows, so split words (decoy names that exist) are presented as the deletion set.
out.splitlines() turns one filename containing a newline into several rows; expand("*") over fixtures "a\nb" and ok.txt returned [a, b, ok.txt].
_walk frames find output line by line (splitlines at 569), so a recursive rm over "dir with space/inner\nname.txt" reports "dir with space/inner" and "name.txt" instead of the real path.
The approved command runs as a single bash -c argument, so shell quoting is honoured and the computed set diverges from the executed set.
decide() snapshots before execution, which bounds the impact to low.
The per-segment note added for run-3 v17 shows the module already treats "the table may be incomplete" as security-relevant; the split-path case produces no note at all.

title: Unauthenticated GET /static/novnc/* runs docker create plus a full /usr/share/novnc tar extraction on every request while home/novnc/core/rfb.js is absent, with no single-flight

root_cause: An unauthenticated static-asset route performs Docker-daemon work and an archive extraction behind a check-then-act test on a single marker file, with no lock, no in-flight flag and no negative cache; exceptions outside the narrow docker-error handlers escape as a 500 without publishing the marker or any bounded negative state, so the expensive state persists and the work is repeatable by any anonymous client.
intended_behavior: Static assets should not require per-request daemon work: the extraction should happen once (at startup or on the first authenticated desktop route) under a lock that lets one caller do it while the others wait or observe the result, and a failed extraction should leave a bounded negative state instead of being retried by every request. /static/novnc/* should answer 404/503 without creating containers whenever the marker is absent.

title: A GUI input queued on gui_lock across a human handback executes with no open burst, so its changes get no snapshot and no gui_changes row
description: AgentBox decides whether a GUI input needs a snapshot before it acquires gui_lock. While a human holds the desktop a takeover lease exists, so GuiBursts.needs_snapshot returns False and the input blocks on gui_lock instead of opening a burst. If the human hands the desktop back while that input is queued, the input runs with a lease check that now passes and no burst open: it writes as uid 1001, calls mark_input, and its fresh input timestamp makes needs_snapshot False for every later input until 60 s of input silence (gui_snapshot_idle) or 600 s after the last snapshot (gui_snapshot_interval). Those inputs produce no snapshot, no burst, and no gui_changes row; the only recovery point predates the human takeover, and the file effects of the inputs are never diffed or attributed.
root_cause: The burst decision is taken outside the lock that serializes execution: service.py:343 evaluates _needs_snapshot (gui_bursts.py:52-63, which returns False while a non-stale lease or pending takeover exists) before _run_tool acquires gui_lock at service.py:136, and the only re-check under the lock (_check_control, service.py:152-161) validates the stale-lease/lease/pending-takeover state, never burst presence. _handback_locked (service.py:528-543) releases the lease (542) and calls forget_input (543) while still holding gui_lock, so the queued input resumes into a state where its earlier premise is gone and nothing takes a snapshot; mark_input (service.py:139) then suppresses the next burst decision.
intended_behavior: Every GUI input that executes must be covered by an open burst bound to a snapshot taken before that input, and each burst must close into a gui_changes record (service.py:261-264 fails closed when a burst baseline cannot be opened; gui_bursts.py:157-162 re-timers lifecycle paths for exactly this reason). A burst decision taken before waiting on a lock must be re-validated after the lock is acquired.

trace.description: Agent token from principal; default_policy.yaml has default: allow and no rule for click/type/key, so GUI inputs are approval-free, are audited as tool_request, and take the ALLOW branch.

_needs_snapshot is evaluated before any lock; while a takeover lease is present _over_snapshot_quota is skipped too and GuiBursts.needs_snapshot returns False, so no snapshot is taken and no burst is opened.
gui_lock is acquired afterwards without a timeout, so an input that already decided 'no burst needed' can sit queued while the human's handback holds the same lock.
The only re-check after acquiring gui_lock handles a stale lease, a live lease and the pending-takeover marker; burst presence and the earlier needs_snapshot result are never re-validated.
While gui_lock is still held, the human handback releases the lease; the queued input then acquires the lock with no lease and no pending marker, so _check_control passes.
forget_input only drops the input timestamp; the handback opens no burst, so the resumed input's decision premise is gone but nothing forces a snapshot.
The resumed input executes the GUI action and calls bursts.mark_input although no burst is open.
The fresh input timestamp makes the next decision False, so later inputs run burstless until gui_snapshot_idle of silence or gui_snapshot_interval since the last snapshot.
Only an open burst is ever diffed and logged as gui_changes; no burst exists for these inputs, so their /workspace changes are never recorded.

evidence.description: Burst decision taken before the lock; with a lease present it is False.
gui_lock is acquired after that decision, with no timeout.
_check_control re-checks only stale lease, lease and pending takeover; no burst-presence condition.
The handback releases the lease inside the gui_lock-held section.
forget_input in the same section clears the timestamp but opens no burst.
needs_snapshot returns False while a non-stale lease or pending takeover exists, assuming the input will get 423.
mark_input runs for an input that has no burst open.
A fresh input timestamp suppresses the following burst decision.
No burst, so no gui_changes row for the changes made by these inputs.
_snap_locks serializes SNAPSHOT_TOOLS, so at most one GUI input per sandbox is in _call_tool at a time; the window is the handback's lock-held section, not a queue of many inputs.
gui_snapshot_idle default 60 s: the burstless window ends after that much input silence.
gui_snapshot_interval default 600 s: upper bound with continuous input, because a snapshot older than that forces a new burst.

title: A restore racing a delete resurrects the deleted sandbox row and re-authorizes the agent token the delete revoked
description: DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} and POST /sandboxes/{sid}/restore each perform an unlocked read-modify-write on the same sandboxes row. If a DELETE completes between the restore's creation of the replacement container and the restore's final status write, the delete reports success and audits 'sandbox_delete', but the restore's last write puts status='running' and the new container_id back on the row. Neither operation rewrites token_hash, and revocation is expressed only as status!='deleted', so the agt_ token the delete revoked resolves to that sid again and its tool calls execute in the replacement container. The snapshots row also survives (delete removes only images), and the running replacement keeps the snapshot image in use, so the best-effort image removal raises and is swallowed. The control plane therefore reports a completed deletion while the sandbox, its /workspace and its agent authority are live again.
root_cause: Lifecycle operations take no per-sandbox lock and re-read nothing. Service.restore_sandbox and Service.delete_sandbox (service.py:462-475) call SandboxManager.restore and SandboxManager.delete (sandbox.py:387-401, 320-332); each reads the row once with _rec, acts, and writes status/container_id unconditionally through _set, which is a bare UPDATE with no status predicate (sandbox.py:234-237). SandboxManager.restore never checks status=='deleted', so its final _set (sandbox.py:398) overwrites the delete's status write (sandbox.py:326) and reinstates the record. Revocation of the agent token is expressed only as status!='deleted' (sandbox.py:216, 221), so the overwritten status silently re-authorizes the original token hash.
intended_behavior: _container (sandbox.py:225-232) and the token lookups (sandbox.py:211-223) treat status=='deleted' as final: a deleted sandbox is unusable and its agent token is invalid. DELETE is the revocation contract (service.py:471-475 logs sandbox_delete, ends the desktop, deletes the container, drops captures). No later or concurrent lifecycle call may reinstate the record, re-point it at a container, or make the revoked token valid again.

The DELETE must complete its row read, status write and image-removal attempt inside the window that opens when the restore's replacement container has been created (sandbox.py:397) and closes at the restore's status write (sandbox.py:398), and the restore must be preempted in that window. So the overlap is reachable but narrow.
The sandbox has at least one snapshot row; DELETE never removes snapshots rows (sandbox.py:327-332 only tries to remove images) and restore accepts any row of that sid.

No special runtime or container capability is needed: the resurrection is decided entirely in the SQLite row and the token lookups. The daemon fact that matters (images.remove refusing while a running container holds the image) is what real Docker does; the harness models it, and even if the image were removed the running replacement and the surviving snapshots row would still leave the sandbox resurrected.

def _lifecycle_lock(self, sid: str) -> threading.Lock:
        with self._busy_lock:
            return self._snap_locks.setdefault("lifecycle:" + sid, threading.Lock())

    def restore_sandbox(self, sid: str, snap_id: str, session: str | None = _NO_SESSION) -> dict[str, Any]:
        with self._lifecycle_lock(sid):
            self.log_human("restore_request", sid, _with_session({"snapshot_id": snap_id}, session))
            self.end_desktop(sid, "sandbox_restored")
            rec = self.sandboxes.restore(sid, snap_id)
            self.bursts.reset_timers(sid)
            self.log_human("restored", sid, _with_session({"snapshot_id": snap_id, "container_id": rec["container_id"]}, session))
            return rec

    def delete_sandbox(self, sid: str, session: str | None = _NO_SESSION) -> None:
        with self._lifecycle_lock(sid):
            self.log_human("sandbox_delete", sid, _with_session({}, session))
            self.end_desktop(sid, "sandbox_deleted")
            self.sandboxes.delete(sid)
            self.drop_captures(sid)

title: Snapshot quota is decided from one container probe, but the docker commit is triggered by a second probe that the quota does not check
description: An agent that holds only its own sandbox's agent token can get docker commits without approval after its sandbox has reached snapshot_quota (default 50). For an ALLOW decision, _call_tool consults _over_snapshot_quota (service.py:298). That function returns False whenever _needs_snapshot is False. For write_file, _needs_snapshot runs sandboxes.exists(), an untimed `test -e` exec inside the agent's own container (service.py:236 -> sandbox.py:458-461). The ALLOW branch then calls _needs_snapshot a second time (service.py:343) and commits on that result without checking the quota again (service.py:345 -> _snapshot -> sandbox.py:355). If the target path appears between the two probes, an over-quota call that should have become REQUIRE_APPROVAL/snapshot-quota becomes an unapproved commit. The agent can make the path appear in two ways. (a) It sends an allowlisted exec `touch <path>` (default_policy.yaml:22-29; touch is on line 27) at the same time as the write. exec is not in SNAPSHOT_TOOLS (service.py:35), so call_tool does not serialize it with the write_file under _snap_locks (service.py:278-285); tool_concurrency allows 4 concurrent calls. (b) Any process running in the container toggles the path. Within one sandbox, _snap_locks only serializes write_file, delete_file and GUI_INPUT calls against each other. The pending-approval cap (PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX=20) does not stop the bypass: it only blocks the REQUIRE_APPROVAL branch. Each commit is a full docker commit of the container (sandbox.py:355-356). config.py:44-46 records why the quota exists: commit copies the whole writable layer, and the quota keeps the agent from filling host disk without a human. Snapshot images are freed only when the sandbox is deleted (sandbox.py:327-332). The marginal harm depends on deployment. With AGENTBOX_DISK set (storage_opt, sandbox.py:263-264), the writable layer is bounded and the quota is the only bound on how many copies of that layer are kept, so the bypass multiplies it without limit. With the default empty AGENTBOX_DISK (config.py:41-42), the agent can already grow the writable layer directly through repeated unapproved write_file calls (1 MiB each, config.py:55), so the bypass mainly adds amplification. Local reproduction used the real AgentBox._call_tool/call_tool, Policy.load(default_policy.yaml), AuditLog and ApprovalStore with a fake SandboxManager. Its exists() stats a real file with a modelled 20 ms probe latency, and exec touch has a modelled 20 ms latency. No Docker was used. Results with the sandbox already at quota=2: a control call on a stably existing path returned 202 pending snapshot-quota with 0 commits. Concurrent agent exec `touch /workspace/pN` started 5 ms before, together with, or 5 ms after write_file gave 20/20 write_file calls returning 200 executed with a snapshot commit each, 0 approvals and policy_decision allow (an offset of -10 ms gave 18/20; -15 ms gave 0/20). A real background thread toggling the file every 2-20 ms produced 9 over-quota commits in 40 calls (7 in an earlier run), alongside 20 pending approvals.
claimed_root_cause: _call_tool reads the same mutable, agent-controlled container state twice: once in _over_snapshot_quota through _needs_snapshot/sandboxes.exists (service.py:298 -> 248 -> 236), then again in the pre-execution _needs_snapshot (service.py:343). It does not compute one 'snapshot needed' decision and bind both the quota gate and the commit to it. The quota therefore guards only the first probe, and the commit at service.py:345 has no quota check of its own. The serialization in _snap_locks covers only SNAPSHOT_TOOLS, so agent tools outside that set (exec) and processes inside the container can change the probed state between the two reads.

trace.description: POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/write_file with the agent token of that sandbox (the only check is p.sandbox_id == sid at api.py:217-218). The call is dispatched to tool_pool and runs box.call_tool (api.py:219-220).
Only SNAPSHOT_TOOLS (write_file/delete_file/GUI_INPUT, service.py:35) take the per-sandbox snap lock. A concurrent exec from the same agent runs unlocked at line 285.
The quota gate is evaluated only for ALLOW decisions (write_file is allowed by default: default_policy.yaml:10). Its boolean only rewrites the decision; nothing is kept for the execution step.
Once snapshot_count >= quota, the result is _needs_snapshot(); if the first probe says 'no snapshot', the call stays ALLOW.
First probe: untimed docker exec `test -e <path>` as the agent uid inside the agent-controlled container (called from service.py:236).
Second _needs_snapshot evaluation on the ALLOW path. The path now exists, so it returns True; the quota is not re-checked.

docker commit of the whole container (pause=True), reached via service.py:345 -> _snapshot (service.py:253). The image is retained until the sandbox is deleted, and a snapshot row is inserted that pushes snapshot_count further past the quota.

evidence.description: _over_snapshot_quota compares snapshot_count with the quota and returns _needs_snapshot(); its result is used only to rewrite the decision at line 298-302.
write_file needs_snapshot is sandboxes.exists(path), a live probe of agent-mutable state; SandboxError is mapped to False.
The ALLOW branch calls _snapshot on the second evaluation and does not consult the quota.
SNAPSHOT_TOOLS = {write_file, delete_file} | GUI_INPUT. exec is excluded, so call_tool (278-285) never serializes it with a write_file in the same sandbox.

The pending-approval cap only applies on the REQUIRE_APPROVAL branch. Calls that win the race take the ALLOW branch, so a full queue (20) does not stop the bypass; in the local run, commits continued alongside 429 responses.
snapshot_count is COUNT(*) of snapshot rows, the only quantity the quota measures.
exists() runs `test -e` through exec_run with no timeout, inside the sandbox the agent controls.
Snapshot images are removed only in delete(); nothing prunes them earlier.
storage_opt size (writable-layer bound) is applied only when disk_limit is set; it is empty by default (config.py:41-42).
touch and mkdir are in the read-only-exec allowlist (rule at 22-29), so the agent can create the path without approval; Policy.decide returns allow/read-only-exec for `touch /workspace/p1`.
default: allow; no rule targets write_file, so Policy.decide returns allow with rule_id null for write_file.

The source comment states the quota's purpose: docker commit copies the whole write layer each time, and the quota keeps the agent from filling host disk without a human (snapshot_quota default 50 at line 46).

blockers: No Docker daemon is available to the audit agents. Win rate and offset tolerance were measured only with modelled 20 ms probe/exec latencies against the real control-plane code. The real interleaving of two docker-exec `test -e` probes, the policy_decision audit write between them, and a concurrent docker-exec `touch` (or an in-container toggling process) has not been observed.

The host-disk effect per bypassed commit (writable-layer size, whether AGENTBOX_DISK/storage_opt is configured and enforced on xfs+pquota, free host disk) is a deployment fact. With the default empty AGENTBOX_DISK, the agent can already grow the writable layer directly through unapproved write_file calls, so the quota bypass matters as a separate bound only where a disk limit is set.
